description_en: Ajayamerukoṭa is situated 4 km north-west of Amargaḍhī, the Dadeldhura district headquarters. Most of the monuments are built on the right bank of the Chaurī Gāḍ river, an affluent of the Mahakali (or Sharda) river, that makes the western river between India and Nepal. The monument is located in an area where are found other contemporary constructions (DDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120).The area of Ajayamerukoṭa is rich in monuments that were mostly erected during the 14th and 15th centuries. According to D. P. Ojha, Ajayamerukoṭa was a local capital of the Khasiya kings from Jumla, (i.e. the Khaśa Malla emperors, 12th-14th century) (Ojha 1989: p. 54). From the mid-14th century, Ajayamerukoṭa seems to have taken greater importance as a capital of the Doti kingdom, especially under the reign of king Niraya Pāla (r. c. 1362-1383 AD). Indeed, it is around Niraya Pāla's time that Doti emerged as an entity independant from the Khaśa Malla empire. This political and economical rise is demonstrated in the numerous monuments erected between the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.TThe monument in question is a pavilion (bhaiṭak) located between two śikhara temples. It consists of four intricately carved stone pillars that support a corbelled dome. The pillars are adorned with carvings ofkalaśamotifs. The outer covering of the dome was likely made with stone tiles, similar to those observed on a nearby pavilion (DDL0120).This architectural style, featuring a central pavilion (maṇḍapa,baiṭhak) flanked by twośikharas, is rarely found in far western Nepal but can be seen at the Bhurtī Temple Complex in Dailekh district (DLK0015). However, there are structural differences between the Bhurtī and Ajayamerukoṭa monuments. In Bhurtī, the pavilion was intentionally integrated as a planned component of the temples, whereas in Ajayamerukoṭa, the pavilion appears as an independent structure. This suggests that the architects in Bhurtī drew inspiration from pre-existing models, such as the Ajayamerukoṭa monuments, which themselves were likely influenced by temples from Uttarakhand.The easternśikhara(DDL0132) contains an inscription dated to 1373 (ŚS 1295) (Sharma 2012, p. 303). This indicates that the pavilion was most likely built during the same period, specifically during the reign of King Niraya Pāla.
references: REFERENCES Ojha, D. P. 1988. Doti Kṣetrako Itihās tathā Saṃnskrīti . Kathmandu: Sudur Paścimāncal Sāmājik Sevā tathā Anusandhān Samiti. Sharma, Dilli Raj. 2012. Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture . Kathmandu: Centre for Nepal and Asian Studies, pp. 302-304.
